title: Machine Learning Basics
description: Core ideas behind training and evaluating machine learning models.

questions.prompt: What does **supervised learning** require that unsupervised learning does not?
questions.explanation: Supervised learning fits a mapping from inputs to known targets, so every training example needs a label. Unsupervised methods such as clustering find structure without labels.

questions.prompt: In gradient descent with learning rate $\eta$, which update moves parameters $\theta$ toward a lower loss $L$?
questions.explanation: The gradient points in the direction of steepest *increase* of the loss, so we step against it: $$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta L(\theta)$$

questions.prompt: Which of these are common techniques for reducing overfitting?
options: Training for more epochs on the same data
questions.explanation: Weight decay, dropout and early stopping all limit how closely a model can fit noise in the training set. Training longer on the same data usually makes overfitting worse.

questions.prompt: It is good practice to tune hyperparameters by repeatedly checking performance on the test set.
questions.explanation: Tuning on the test set leaks information about it into your choices, so the final score becomes optimistic. Use a separate validation set (or cross-validation) for tuning and touch the test set once.

questions.prompt: A model has low training error but much higher validation error. What is the most likely problem?
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and validation error is the classic sign of high variance: the model memorized training specifics that do not generalize.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a validation set?
options: Choose model settings before final testing
questions.explanation: Validation data guides model selection and hyperparameter tuning; a held-out test set is reserved for final evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe k-fold cross-validation?
options: The data is split into k folds
Each fold serves as validation once
It guarantees an unbiased score after tuning on all folds
questions.explanation: Each fold takes a turn as validation while the others train the model. Repeated tuning can still overfit these estimates.

questions.prompt: For a binary classifier, what does changing the decision threshold usually change?
questions.explanation: A threshold changes which scores are labeled positive, shifting precision and recall without retraining the model.

questions.prompt: A feature measured only after the outcome occurs can cause target leakage when used for prediction.
questions.explanation: Such a feature reveals information unavailable at prediction time, making offline performance misleading.

questions.prompt: For a rare positive class, which metric is often more informative than accuracy?
questions.explanation: Accuracy can look high by predicting only the majority class. Precision and recall expose performance on the rare class.

questions.prompt: What does standardization commonly do to a feature?
options: Subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation
Convert every value to a class label
questions.explanation: Z-score standardization centers a feature and scales it by its spread; it does not guarantee normality or remove outliers.

questions.prompt: A strong correlation between two variables by itself proves that one causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation can arise from confounding, coincidence, or reverse causality; causal claims need stronger designs or assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which approaches combine predictions from multiple models?
questions.explanation: Bagging, boosting, and voting combine learners in different ways. Feature scaling alone does not create an ensemble.

questions.prompt: What does ROC AUC summarize?
questions.explanation: ROC AUC measures how well positive examples rank above negatives across thresholds; it does not directly assess calibration.

questions.prompt: What is a typical goal of clustering?
options: Group examples by similarity without provided class labels
questions.explanation: Clustering organizes unlabeled examples according to a chosen similarity or distance measure.

questions.prompt: Which practices help prevent leakage when evaluating a model?
options: Fit normalization using training data only
Keep related duplicate records in different splits
Use time-aware splits for future prediction
questions.explanation: Preprocessing must learn only from training data; related records should stay together, and temporal tasks need realistic chronological splits.

questions.prompt: What can happen when regularization is made excessively strong?
questions.explanation: Strong constraints can prevent the model from capturing genuine patterns, causing high bias and underfitting.

questions.prompt: A calibrated model that predicts 0.8 for many cases should be correct on roughly 80% of those cases.
questions.explanation: Calibration compares predicted probabilities with empirical frequencies among predictions of similar confidence.

questions.prompt: Compared with squared-error loss, what is a common property of mean absolute error?
options: It is less sensitive to large residuals
It is always differentiable at zero
questions.explanation: Absolute error grows linearly with residual magnitude, so extreme errors have less influence than under squared error.

questions.prompt: What is distribution shift in deployed machine learning?
options: The input or target data distribution changes from training conditions
A feature is renamed in documentation
questions.explanation: Changing real-world data conditions can reduce performance even when the deployed model code is unchanged.
